title: Nobody's Roof
logline: An open wooden hall with no walls and no door stands at the edge of a farming village, raised on four stones, built three centuries ago by people nobody can name so that strangers walking a long road would have somewhere dry to sit, and it is still there, still open, and empty most of the day.
human_question: What is left of a piece of goodness once everyone involved in it is gone?

place.what_kind_of_place: A small open-sided hall of timber at the edge of a village of coconut and paddy, standing now in a swept compound of its own with a low boundary fence and a sand apron around it, where a narrow lane runs off toward the fields. It has no walls, no door and nothing inside it. Four round boulders, set in from the corners, carry four enormous squared sills that are at once the base of the building and its benches, so the wood never touches the ground. Nine short posts inside are octagonal, with a square panel reserved at mid-height, and every one of those panels is carved; a ring of plainer outer posts stands around them, seventeen or nineteen of them depending on who did the counting. Above, thirty-two rafters run up and are locked together by one large carved wooden pin, and a rod driven through openings in the rafters holds their alignment. The whole thing is tiled, and small: the floor is about twelve feet by nine, and the ridge is under twelve feet off the ground. It was put up on a footpath between two old capitals, one of a chain of such halls set two to three miles apart along the same route, with a water pot set out in front and a well of stacked clay rings somewhere near. The path is a village road now. The hall belongs to no household, is locked to nobody, and was built for people who would pass once and never be seen again.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: It is a building whose whole subject is absence, and it is also the most heavily carved thing of its kind anywhere in the country. There is nothing in it, and it is still the most carefully made object for miles: thirty-six carved panels on nine posts, and then more on the corbels, the beams and the rafters — dancers, drummers, a pair of wrestlers cut so the panel reads the same way upside down, lions, elephants, peacocks, deer, and cobras running through the whole building, forty-odd of them, with four serpents coiling up the one round post and cobra hoods standing in for the petals of a lotus. It is a film of surfaces at close range, and a film of light: because there are no walls, the building is made of light and the fields are visible straight through it in every direction. The one great structural image is inside, not above — thirty-two rafters converging on a single pin, seen from below, under a tiled roof that hides them completely from the air. When rain comes it becomes the loudest place in the village for twenty minutes and then goes quiet again.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Light, weather and whoever happens to be walking. The hall has no schedule of its own: it fills for the length of a shower, or for the half hour somebody waits out the middle of the day, and empties again. Around it the fields change through a season, from flooded to green to gold to stubble, and the lane carries different traffic at different hours. Nothing in the film can be arranged except the hour and the weather.
place.when_it_looks_best: The first weeks of a monsoon, when showers arrive in the afternoon and the hall is actually used, and the fields around it are at their most saturated. Within a day: first light, when the carving is raking and the village is quiet; the vertical noon shot on the roof hub; and last light, when the building is a dark frame with fields showing through it.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about a small perfect building and the weather that goes through it. Wood, stone, rain, the light moving across carved pillars across a day, fields visible straight through the middle of a house, a roof seen from above as a wheel of thirty-two spokes, and the long stretches when there is nobody in it at all. Anyone who likes buildings, or likes watching weather arrive, has a complete piece here with nothing said over it.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same hall becomes the sources' account of ordinary goodness, standing in a field. The texts hold that the kind of good mind most people actually have is called great not because it is lofty but because it is common: it is everywhere, in ordinary people, in every place. This building is that claim in timber. Nobody's name is on it. Nobody is being kind in it. It is an arrangement that gives shelter to whoever turns up, and goes on doing it long after everyone who made it is dead, which is the only way a camera can honestly look at generosity at all.

sequence.on_screen: First light, very high and straight down. A village of coconut and paddy, a lane, water in the fields, and at the edge of it one small dark rectangle of roof with nothing built against it.
sequence.voice: Somebody put this up about three hundred years ago beside a footpath, so that people walking a long way would have a roof. There is no record of who. There is nothing in it. It has never been anybody's.

sequence.on_screen: Ground level, slow: the four boulders at the corners, the beams laid across stone, the feet of the pillars, the seventeen outer columns, the nine carved inner ones. Light coming through from every side because there are no walls.
sequence.voice: The old analysis of mind says that awareness never arrives on its own. It comes with a small crew that starts at the same instant, finishes at the same instant, attends to the same thing and stands on the same support [C019-P:L33–L47]. Nothing here holds anything up by itself either.

sequence.on_screen: Drone directly overhead, descending onto the roof: thirty-two rafters running up to one wooden hub. Held long. Then inside, looking up at the same hub from below.
sequence.voice: The texts are careful about the count. There are fifty-two of these companions on the list, and a given moment takes only the ones its work needs, as few as seven and never more than thirty-six [C019-P:L49]. A roof is not built out of every piece of timber in the world. It is built out of exactly what this roof requires.

sequence.on_screen: Rain arriving across the fields. Two or three people come in off the lane without hurrying, sit on the beams, wait. Nobody speaks much. Filmed wide and from behind, as weather rather than as portraiture. The rain stops and they go.
sequence.voice: The sources count eight ordinary good minds, made by three simple differences: glad, or level and unexcited; understanding what you are doing, or just doing it because it is what is done; arriving by itself, or only after somebody asked. All eight are counted as fully good [C011-M:L3]. They rank the unprompted one a little higher, and then say plainly that this is a secondary matter [C011-M:L28].

sequence.on_screen: The carving, close and in sequence: a dancer, a wrestler mid-hold, a bird, a coiled serpent, a flower repeating around a pillar. Then pull back to show that all this is holding up a roof over an empty floor.
sequence.voice: One source makes a strange point about the name. This kind of goodness is called great not because it is the highest kind, but because it is common: it turns up everywhere, in ordinary people, in every place [C011-M:L16]. The rare and deep states belong to very few. The account of goodness starts in the doorway, not on the mountain.

sequence.on_screen: The lane running away from the hall through the fields. An old well under trees. Ordinary traffic at different hours of one day, compressed: a bicycle, a tractor, schoolchildren, a man with a mammoty, nobody stopping.
sequence.voice: Giving is one of the plain acts the sources say this mind arises in, along with keeping your word, helping, listening, teaching [C011-P:L51]. And they are strict about the unit. A good day is not one long good mood. These minds come in moments, in the intervals when someone is actually attending to what they are doing, with other things running in between [C011-P:L111].

sequence.on_screen: Last light. The empty hall from the lane, fields showing straight through it. Then dark, and the shape of the roof against a sky with some light left in it.
sequence.voice: A camera cannot see which state of mind anybody was in, then or now, and this film does not claim to. What it can show is the arrangement: a roof, four stones, a bench, no door, and nobody to thank.

concept_merge.why_together: C011 supplies the claim and its scale. The sources teach eight ordinary wholesome minds, produced by three yes-or-no differences — joyful or evenly neutral, with or without the understanding of action and its results, arising by itself or only after being prompted [C011-M:L3] — and they list giving, helping, keeping precepts, listening and teaching as the plain acts these minds arise in [C011-P:L51]. Then comes the line the whole film is built on: this goodness is called great because it is common to many, everywhere, not because it stands above anything [C011-M:L16]. C019 supplies the structure that keeps the building from being a metaphor for a person. A mind never arrives alone; its companions begin together, end together, take one object and rest on one support [C019-P:L33–L47], and only as many of them arrive as the work requires, between seven and thirty-six [C019-P:L49]. Put on an open hall built for strangers, the two stop being doctrine and become a description of what is standing there: an assembly of parts, none of which does anything alone, arranged to give something away to people it will never meet.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That generosity can be read off a structure instead of a face, and that this is not a compromise but the more accurate reading. C011 on its own would ask a camera to show which mind somebody was in, which no camera can do. C019 on its own would be an inventory. Together on a building whose only purpose is to shelter whoever turns up, they show that the tradition's 'great' goodness is exactly the unremarkable kind — so common it can be left by the road, unlocked, for three hundred years, and used without anybody noticing it is a gift.

concept_links.why: The digest gives eight ordinary wholesome minds produced by three differences, joyful or evenly neutral, with or without the understanding of action and its results, spontaneous or prompted, and counts all eight as genuinely good [C011-M:L3]; it lists giving and helping among the acts such a mind arises in [C011-P:L51]; and it carries the claim that makes this film possible, that this goodness is called great because it is common to many and everywhere, not because it is higher [C011-M:L16]. Every limit in the digest that bears on this film is honoured on screen. The film never suggests that a gift only counts if the giver was glad, since a mind accompanied by neutral feeling is fully wholesome and joy depends on conditions [C011-P:L57–L66]; it never suggests that having to be asked cancels the act, which the sources rank only as a secondary difference [C011-M:L28]; it never treats the size of a gift as the measure of a giver, because the sources' coin-and-note comparison is one giver on two days, not a rich giver against a poor one [C011-M:L26]; and it does not let 'understanding' slide into education or cleverness, which the Pradeepika explicitly rejects [C011-P:L70]. The warning that a devotional day is not one unbroken good mind, that these minds come only in moments of attention with other things between them [C011-P:L111], is spoken aloud rather than smoothed over.

The digest's four marks of association — arising together, ceasing together, one object, one base [C019-P:L33–L47] — are what let a building stand in for an assembly without becoming a diagram of a soul, and the rule that only the needed factors arise, from seven to at most thirty-six [C019-P:L49], is spoken over the one shot where the count is literally visible. The digest's corrections are load-bearing and are kept. The film never presents the parts as persistent agents or inner selves, because the factors arise and cease with each moment. It never says or implies that every good moment contains all fifty-two: the group's shorthand about the team that travels with each mind means the roster, not the attendance. And it does not treat craft skill as a morally neutral tool, since the source holds that the common factors take the whole quality of the mind they join, like a friend who follows the company he keeps [C019-P:L61–L63].

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the goodness these texts call great is the ordinary kind, common everywhere, and that it can be built into an arrangement and left behind — so that what survives of a good act is not a reputation but a roof that anybody may sit under, made of parts none of which does anything on its own.
what_must_be_real: The building as it actually stands, including its repairs, its modern fittings and whatever state of upkeep it is really in. Nobody is asked to walk in, sit down, shelter or leave for the camera, and nobody who does come in is presented as an example of anything; if the hall is empty for a week, the film is of an empty hall for a week. The carving is not lit or dressed to look older or finer than it is. No claim is made on camera about who built it or why, beyond what is actually known, which is very little. Filming inside a protected monument happens on the terms of whoever is responsible for it, and nothing is moved, cleaned or touched.
position_hint: opening: it is the group's plainest statement that this goodness is the common kind, and it needs no other concept in place before it. It should come before the films that describe what a good mind is made of, because they all assume the claim this one makes.
risks: Turning the builders into unnamed saints. The sources describe moments of mind, not kinds of person, and nothing is known about whoever put this up.

Elegy. C061 bars legacy and remembrance framing outright, and nearly every popular account of a wayside hall is exactly that: a lament for a vanished age of village virtue, a lost craft, a hospitality nobody practises any more. This film refuses all of it. It is not about a tradition that has gone, not about what has been forgotten, and not about decline. What is standing is a maintained object in the present tense — retiled in 2016, most of its carved timber replaced and copied in the 1960s, looked after by the village and a district archaeology office — and the voice says so rather than mourning.
Presenting anyone who shelters here as an illustration of goodness, or reading a state of mind off a face, which the digests say repeatedly cannot be done.

Narrating the carving as evidence of a golden age of craft, or as a skill that has been lost. The sources are explicit that much of the visible carving is 1960s replication on new timber, that the removed originals are in a museum in another district, and that some corbels were finished more simply than the originals because the money ran out. Filming honey-coloured replacement timber as three-hundred-year-old work would be a lie the camera tells by itself.

Letting the skill of the work stand in for the understanding the sources mean. The Pradeepika rejects exactly that slide: craft and learning are not the knowledge that makes a good mind good [C011-P:L70].
Implying that a larger or grander gift makes a better giver; the sources' comparison is one giver on two days, not one giver against another [C011-M:L26].

Suggesting that giving reluctantly, or only after being asked, does not count [C011-M:L28]. The research makes this live rather than theoretical: the record does not say whether this hall was endowed, volunteered or expected, and the doctrine says the question is secondary.

Quietly dropping the sources' insistence that these minds are defined partly by their future results [C011-P:L51] and replacing it with wellbeing language, or going the other way and reducing kindness to a transaction.
Narrating the fifty-two factors as though all of them turn up at once, when the sources cap a single moment at thirty-six [C019-P:L49].
Making a heritage film about wood carving, which is a real and separate subject and would swallow this one.

Shooting for an image that does not exist. The roof is tiled and hipped with deep eaves; from above there is no wheel of rafters to see, only tiles and tree canopy. The convergence is an interior shot.
drop_if: The building is closed, under scaffolding or otherwise unfilmable during the window available.
Permission to film a protected monument, or to fly over it, cannot be had.
The only way to show it in use is to arrange for people to sit in it.
The conserved compound turns out to be fenced and kept shut, so that the hall is no longer open to whoever turns up — which would take the film's premise away rather than complicate it.

connections.note: Two giving arrangements at opposite scales: one built once and left standing for centuries, one refilled by somebody different every morning.
This film watches giving after the givers are gone; that one watches it become practised in the hands of people still doing it.

selection.reason: It carries the group's founding claim, that this goodness is great because it is common, on a structure that gives without anybody in frame being a benefactor.

review.note: Still pending. Rewritten 2026-09-22 into the footage-led shape; the old subject, a household that feeds passing strangers, was dropped entirely because it made identifiable people into moral exemplars on camera. Research pass 2026-09-26 added a full historical_thread on the building and on the wayside-hall institution, and corrected the location block where the research changed what is true. logline, two_layers, sequence and concept_merge were left untouched as instructed, but two things in them now need Chathura's judgement. (1) The sequence's first and third beats call for a drone directly overhead reading the roof as a wheel of thirty-two rafters. That image does not exist: the roof is tiled, hipped and deeply eaved, the building is about twelve feet by nine under shade trees, and the rafter convergence can only be filmed from inside looking up. place, why_here and what_to_film have been rebuilt from the ground accordingly; the beats have not. (2) The logline's 'three hundred years ago' sits at the young end of a range of datings that runs from about the eighteenth century back through 'before the sixteenth century' in the Archaeological Commissioner's own consolidation entry to a folk attribution to the thirteenth. No single date is established, so the logline was not changed, but the voice should not sound more certain than the record. The premise that nobody can be named survives the test: no builder, donor, patron or date is recorded anywhere consulted.

suggested_location.name: Panavitiya Ambalama, at the edge of Panavitiya village near Narammala

also_known_as.name: ambalama
also_known_as.meaning: a wayside hall built so that travellers, pilgrims and traders have somewhere to rest

also_known_as.name: madol kurupawa
also_known_as.meaning: the central wooden hub at the apex of the roof, into which the rafters are fixed

suggested_location.region: Kurunegala District, North Western Province: the coconut and paddy country a few kilometres off the Negombo–Kurunegala road, reached by a small road turning off before the town of Narammala
suggested_location.why_here: It puts the concept and the best image in one frame, and the research strengthens rather than decorates the argument. The building exists for one reason: to shelter people who are passing through and will not be seen again, which is generosity built into a structure rather than performed by a person, and is the only form of it this series can honestly film. It is also, by some distance, the most heavily carved surviving hall of its kind in the country — thirty-six carved panels on nine posts, cobras through the whole building, a pair of wrestlers cut to read the same way upside down, sixteen-petalled lotuses on the corbels — so the film's strongest visual material is close, raking and handheld rather than aerial. Thirty-two rafters locked into a single pin give the supporting concept its literal picture of an assembly in which no part does anything alone, and that picture is got from inside, looking up, not from a drone. Above all, it is not one shed: it is one surviving link in a road-long chain of free halls spaced two to three miles apart, with a word for the institution in a seventh-century inscription and seven older names for it in the literature — which is exactly the claim the primary concept makes, that this goodness is called great because it is common and everywhere rather than because it is high.

historical_thread.story:
An ambalama is a wayside hall: a roofed, open-sided shelter put up beside a road so that anyone walking could sit, sleep, wait out rain and drink water, with nothing to pay. The institution is older than any surviving building. A seventh-century rock inscription at Hindagala in Kandy District uses the word paṭasala, which S. Paranavitana (1958) glossed as meaning an ambalama; some scholars read the catussālā of the inscriptions — a hall enterable from four sides — the same way (Geiger 1964; Vidanapatirana 2008). The Cūlavaṃsa is cited for King Vijayabāhu I (1055–1110) building sālā for pilgrims walking to Sri Pada, and later kings for doing the same. Older Sinhala usage calls these halls isimbuhal, māwat maḍu, āgantuka śālā, ambara, maḍam, ambili and ambē; the Ummagga Jātaka, the Saddharmaratnāvaliya and the sandesa poems mention them, the Sælalihini Sandeśaya of 1437 naming a Val-Ambalama beside a water pool on the Kotte–Kelaniya road and the fifteenth-century Gira Sandeśaya one at Velitota near Bentota. They were built beside public highways, at the edges of paddy tracts, under trees and on small rises — old roads ran along the field boundaries, which is why a rest hall so often stands looking at a paddy tract.

Nobody paid to use one. Who built them is described in the sources in two ways that do not quite agree: a wealthy family or a local chieftain endowing and maintaining one, and the village raising one with its own hands because sheltering a tired traveller was a meritorious act. Ananda Coomaraswamy (1962) adds what the hall was for when nobody was travelling — news was exchanged and betel chewed there, the gam sabhā, the village council, sat in it, games were played in it, and the village's revenue was collected in it — and accounts add that seating inside went by age, standing and sometimes caste. Robert Knox, nineteen years a prisoner in the Kandyan kingdom, is quoted for 'places built for strangers and way-faring men to lodge in'. And Wasana Sirimalwatta (2005) names who was on the road: these halls were built especially for the use of people travelling far on rājakāriya — the compulsory service owed to the king under the land-tenure system the British abolished in 1832 — as well as for kin visits and pilgrimages. Many had a pin-tāliya, a water pot set out in front, and an ūrā kæṭa well of stacked clay rings nearby.

The hall at Panavitiya, in Mayurāvatī Korale of the Devamedi Hatpattuwa in Kurunegala District, is the most heavily carved of the survivors. Its floor is a quadrangular platform of packed pebble and broken stone raised about half a foot, 12 feet 4 inches by 9 feet 6 inches; on it four round boulders about a foot high carry four great squared timber sills, set in from the edges, which are at once the base of the building and its benches and which keep the wood clear of damp and termites. Nine inner posts carry the roof and a ring of plainer outer posts stands around them. Each inner post is cut octagonal with a square panel reserved at mid-height, and each panel is carved: thirty-six panels in all. Thirty-two rafters run up and are locked together by one large carved wooden pin, the maḍol kurupāva, forming the kæṇimaḍala, the cone of the roof; a rod called an idda passes through openings in the rafters to hold their alignment. Two carved ridge beams cross above. The roof is tiled, and the posts meet it through carved corbels, pekada.

Rohitha Dasanayake's catalogue of the carvings counts, among the human figures, four dancing women, two dancers, two drummers, two flute players, two conch blowers, two mahouts, two women offering flowers or exchanging greetings, and two angampora wrestlers cut so that the pair reads the same way when the panel is turned upside down. Among the animals: eight lions, four elephants, three peacocks, two deer, one garuḍa and one small bird. Cobras run through the building — seven nāga figures, thirty-six hooded heads, one cobra knot — and on the circular north pillar, the finest post in the hall, four serpents coil up the shaft and four cobra hoods take the place of the petals of the lotus. Then forty bo-leaves, fifteen lotus flowers, twelve creepers, twelve rope-knots, seven mat-weave patterns, and corbels each carrying a sixteen-petalled lotus. Charles Godakumbura noticed something unusual for Kandyan-period work: almost nothing here is mythical, the garuḍa being the only imaginary creature in the building. He and Dasanayake do not agree on everything — what Dasanayake lists as a demon Godakumbura identifies as a masked dancer — and the arithmetic does not close either, one study's text giving forty-five cobra carvings where its own table adds to forty-four.

Who made it is not recorded. There is no builder's name, no donor, no inscription and no date on the building. Two folk traditions attempt it: one holds that the hall was raised in the Dambadeniya period, though its carpentry belongs squarely to the Kandyan; the other that it was made by the son of the craftsman who built the Magul Maduwa, the royal audience hall at Kandy, after the two quarrelled and separated, the father building the king's hall and the son this one — and, in the darker version, that a fault in the driving of the idda killed them both when they met again.

By 1960 the building was in bad condition. The Archaeological Commissioner's administration report for 1960–61 records that the cone at the apex had broken and the rafters had come apart, and that the roof was then thatched with coconut frond. Charles Godakumbura's department consolidated it between 1960 and 1963: decayed members were taken down and their carvings copied onto new timber of the same species, the removed originals were chemically treated and sent to the museum at Anuradhapura, plastic wood was used to make good what survived, and — the report says so plainly — some replacement corbels were finished in a simpler style than the originals because of cost. Tile fragments of three kinds, found scattered in the ground during the work, established that the roof had been tiled from the beginning, so it was tiled again. A buried stone revetment came to light as the ground was cleared and was rebuilt. A granite base was later built around the four original boulders to protect them. The hall was conserved again in 2016; a photograph from June 2017 shows it under a wholly fresh skin of tiles with a stack of spares beside it. It is listed as a protected monument, is maintained under the department's Dambadeniya archaeological office, and carries a signboard at the site setting out the stages of its restoration.

The road is mostly gone as a road. The Venerable Galagama Aththadassī (2000) traced a Dambadeniya-period footpath running from the east gate of the Dambadeniya palace north-east past Wīrē Ambalama, then to this hall, then on past Deekirikǣwa and Karagahagedara Ambalama to Yapahuwa; L.K. Karunaratne (1971) reported another old route from here towards Anuradhapura, and older villagers hold that a road to Yapahuwa and Kurunegala ran along the paddy tract in front of the building. The halls on such routes stood roughly two to three miles apart. Of the three named on that path, this one stands and is protected; Karagahagedara stands on a rock shelf above a paddy tract and is on the same protected list; and Wīrē Ambalama is gone, though villagers still call the land where it stood ambalamē kǣlla, the ambalama plot. A fourth hall in the district, Bōgahapitiya, built in 1782 and entered in the Department of Cultural Affairs' 1972 register of ancient monuments as finely carved, has not even ruins left. The modern roads between those two old capitals do not pass this hall; it is reached now by a village road turning off the Girīulla–Kurunegala road at Matiyagane junction, or off the Narammala–Kuliyapitiya road at Dangolla.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The history sharpens the film's argument on the exact axis the primary concept already contains. C011 sorts the eight everyday wholesome minds by three yes-or-no differences, and one of them is whether the mind arose by itself or only after somebody prompted it [C011-M:L3]. The sources on this institution divide on precisely that: some accounts have a wealthy family or a local chieftain endowing and maintaining a hall, others have the village raising one with its own hands as a meritorious act, and for this particular building the record says neither. That would be a hole in a film built on spontaneous giving. It is not a hole in this one, because the digest settles the matter in the opposite direction from the sentimental reading: a prompted wholesome mind is fully wholesome, and the ranking between prompted and unprompted is explicitly a secondary matter [C011-M:L28]. A duty discharged is not thereby not a kindness. The film therefore does not have to decide whether anyone wanted to build this, which is fortunate, because the record cannot decide it and a camera certainly cannot.

The documented obligation, in fact, runs the other way round, and that is the better image. What is recorded is not that the halls were built under compulsion but that they were built for people walking under it: these shelters were put up especially for travellers going far on rājakāriya, the service owed to the king, as well as for kin visits and pilgrimage. So the road these buildings stand on was full of people doing what they had to do, and the bench was free. That is the sources' own list of plain acts — giving, helping, listening, keeping one's word, teaching [C011-P:L51] — arranged along a road rather than performed in a face, and it is the only register in which a camera can film generosity at all.

Then the line the whole film rests on. C011 says this goodness is called great not because it stands above anything but because it is common to many, everywhere, in ordinary people, in every place [C011-M:L16]. That claim is not a claim about one building; it is a claim about a distribution, and the research turns it into one that can be photographed and counted. Halls every two to three miles along a walking route. Three of them named on this one footpath. A word for the institution in a seventh-century inscription, seven older names for it in the literature, halls in the sandesa poems and in the Jātaka stories, one heritage gazetteer's ambalama category running to a hundred and eighty-four entries. The film's single location is a sample, not a monument, and the voice can say so without leaving the frame.

C019 keeps the building from becoming a portrait. Its four marks of association — arising together, ceasing together, one object, one base [C019-P:L33–L47] — are what the roof is: thirty-two rafters that stand only because they are locked into one pin, with a rod through them to hold their alignment, so that nothing in the assembly does anything alone and nothing outlasts the rest of it. The count is exact and finite, which is the rule the digest states: only as many factors as the work requires, between seven and thirty-six, never the whole roster [C019-P:L49]. And the ethically variable factors, which take the whole quality of the mind they join like a friend who follows the company he keeps [C019-P:L61–L63], are the carpentry itself: the folk story about this hall says the same hands and the same training built a king's audience chamber and a shed for strangers, and the skill was indifferent between them.

What the history does not license has to be said as firmly as what it does. It gives no evidence whatever about anybody's state of mind. Thirty-six carved panels are not proof of devotion, a joint is not proof of generosity, and the digests are explicit that no camera can show which factor was present. The Pradeepika also rules out the nearest cheat, reading the skill of the work as the understanding that makes a mind good [C011-P:L70]. The film must not become an argument that the builders were good people. It is an argument about an arrangement: a roof, four stones, a bench, no door, no charge, and nobody to thank.

Finally, this is the history that keeps the film off elegy, which is the live danger, since almost every popular account of a wayside hall is a lament for a vanished age of village virtue and C061 bars legacy and remembrance framing outright. Two things prevent it. The first is in the record: what stands here is not a survival, it is a repair. Most of the carved timber was replaced and copied in the early 1960s, the originals are in a museum a long way off, some corbels were deliberately finished more plainly because the money ran out, the roof was renewed in 2016, and a district office and a village keep it. That is maintenance in the present tense. The second is in the doctrine: these minds arise only in moments of attention with other things running between them [C011-P:L111], so there was never a good century to mourn any more than there was a good day. The film is not about what has been lost. It is about a thing that is still there, still open, and still being looked after.
historical_thread.what_is_certain:
That an ambalama is a free open-sided wayside rest hall and that no charge was made for using one. That the hall at Panavitiya stands in Mayurāvatī Korale of the Devamedi Hatpattuwa, Kurunegala District, above a paddy tract, and that it is reached by a village road off the Girīulla–Kurunegala road at Matiyagane junction or off the Narammala–Kuliyapitiya road at Dangolla. That it stands on four round boulders about a foot high, set in from the corners of a stone-filled platform raised about half a foot from the ground, and that four great squared timber sills laid across those boulders serve both as structure and as seating. That the platform is recorded as 12 feet 4 inches by 9 feet 6 inches, the roof as 18 feet 3 inches by 16 feet 6 inches, and the height to the ridge as 11 feet 5 inches. That nine inner posts carry the roof, that they are octagonal with a square panel reserved at mid-height, and that there are thirty-six carved panels in all. That the roof has thirty-two rafters locked by a single carved wooden pin called the maḍol kurupāva, that a rod called an idda passes through openings in the rafters, that there are two carved ridge beams, and that the posts meet the roof through carved corbels bearing sixteen-petalled lotuses. That the roof is tiled. That the carvings include dancers, drummers, flute and conch players, mahouts, women greeting or offering flowers, a pair of angampora wrestlers cut to read the same way inverted, lions, elephants, peacocks, deer, a garuḍa, a great many cobras and cobra hoods, bo-leaves, lotuses, creepers, rope-knots and mat-weave patterns, and that one inner post on the north side is circular rather than octagonal, with four serpents coiling up it and cobra hoods in place of lotus petals. That Rohitha Dasanayake published a tabulated count of them and Charles Godakumbura described and photographed them for the Department of Archaeology. That Godakumbura remarked on the near-absence of mythical creatures, the garuḍa excepted.

That the 1960–61 administration report of the Archaeological Commissioner records the building as very dilapidated, the cone at the apex broken, the rafters parted and the roof thatched with coconut frond. That the Department of Archaeology consolidated it between 1960 and 1963 under Godakumbura; that decayed members were dismantled and their carvings replicated on new timber of the same species; that the removed originals were chemically treated and sent to the Anuradhapura museum; that plastic wood was used on surviving timber; and that some replacement corbels were finished in a simpler style than the originals for reasons of cost. That tile fragments of three kinds found in the ground during the work established that the roof had been tiled originally. That a buried stone revetment was uncovered and rebuilt, and that a granite base was later built around the four original boulders. That the hall was conserved again in 2016. That it carries a Department of Archaeology signboard showing the stages of the restoration, and is maintained under the department's Dambadeniya office.

That halls of this kind were built beside public highways, at the edges of paddy tracts, under trees and on small rises, and that on this route they stood roughly two to three miles apart. That Ven. Galagama Aththadassī traced a Dambadeniya-period footpath from the east gate of the Dambadeniya palace north-east past Wīrē Ambalama, this hall, Deekirikǣwa and Karagahagedara Ambalama to Yapahuwa; that Karagahagedara Ambalama still stands and is on the same protected-monuments list; and that Wīrē Ambalama has gone, while the land where it stood is still called ambalamē kǣlla, the ambalama plot. That another carved hall in the district, Bōgahapitiya, is recorded as built in 1782 and entered in the Department of Cultural Affairs' 1972 register of ancient monuments, and that nothing of it now remains. That the older literature calls such halls isimbuhal, māwat maḍu, āgantuka śālā, ambara, maḍam, ambili and ambē, and that they appear in the Ummagga Jātaka, the Saddharmaratnāvaliya and the sandesa poems, the Sælalihini Sandeśaya of 1437 naming a Val-Ambalama on the Kotte–Kelaniya road. That Paranavitana glossed paṭasala in the seventh-century Hindagala inscription as meaning an ambalama. That Coomaraswamy records such halls as the seat of the village council, a place for exchanging news and chewing betel, a place for games, and the office where village revenue was collected. That Sirimalwatta records them as built especially for travellers going far on rājakāriya, on kin visits or on pilgrimage. That rājākariya was a system of land held in return for service to the king, including labour on public works, and that it was abolished in 1832 following the Colebrooke–Cameron reforms. That no builder, donor, patron, village committee or construction date is named for this hall in any source consulted.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed:
The date, above all, and the sources should be kept apart rather than averaged. The Philatelic Bureau's note, followed by the encyclopaedia entry, says it was erected 'in the 18th century or before'. A heritage gazetteer attributes it, on the stylistic features of its carvings, to a period before or during the eighteenth century, and an archaeological article says the carvings are reckoned to belong to about the eighteenth century CE. The architecture is generally assigned to the Kandyan period. But the Archaeological Commissioner's own 1960–61 consolidation entry — Godakumbura's department, the people who took the building apart — describes it as belonging to a period before the sixteenth century. And folk tradition puts it in the Dambadeniya period, three centuries earlier again, which the carpentry does not support. One widely read popular article attributes the hall to King Parākramabāhu II; that is almost certainly a transfer from Giruwa Ambalama, which is attributed to Queen Sunethradevi, his chief consort, and it is recorded here as a warning rather than repeated as a claim. The film's 'three hundred years ago' sits at the young end of a range that runs back to the thirteenth century.

The count of posts. Godakumbura's ICOMOS chapter, followed by the encyclopaedia, gives twenty-eight posts in all, nine inner and nineteen outer, the inner about six feet high and the outer about five and a half. An archaeology site and a heritage gazetteer give twenty-six in all, nine inner and seventeen outer, and put the inner posts at about seven feet, another account at six feet two inches and the outer at five feet eight. The film's 'seventeen or nineteen' keeps the disagreement rather than choosing.

The dimensions. Two sources give the platform as 12 feet 4 inches by 9 feet 6 inches; a third gives roughly 5.5 by 3.7 metres, which is 18 by 12 feet and looks like the roof footprint rather than the floor. Which measurement belongs to which element is not resolved.

The carving counts do not reconcile even inside one study. Its text says forty-five cobra carvings; its own table gives seven nāga figures, thirty-six hoods and one knot, which is forty-four, and separately notes four serpents coiling the round post. Secondary renderings of the same table give forty-nine bo-leaves where the table gives forty, and three rope carvings where the table gives twelve. The number of drummers is given as two in the table and three in one retelling. And the identifications differ: what Dasanayake catalogues as a demon, Godakumbura reads as a masked dancer.

The builder. Nothing is recorded. Two folk traditions compete — construction in the Dambadeniya period, and construction by the son of the craftsman of the royal audience hall at Kandy after a quarrel with his father — and the second has two endings, one of which kills them both over a fault in the driving of the roof pin. A commenter on one archaeological article asks the obvious question, whether a building this laborious can really have been for resting alone or whether it commemorated somebody powerful; no source answers it.

The protected status. The hall appears on the published list of Archaeological Protected Monuments in Kurunegala District under the Narammala divisional secretariat, but, unlike most entries on that list, with no gazette notification number and no date; the citation given is the Department of Archaeology's own site listing. Karagahagedara Ambalama is in the same position. Whether either has been formally gazetted is not established here, although conservation by the department is not in doubt.

How many ambalamas survive is not established anywhere. One heritage gazetteer's ambalama category held a hundred and eighty-four entries when consulted, but that listing includes halls that no longer exist; another catalogues them province by province; the encyclopaedia names fifteen prominent ones. A separate claim, that the last examples remained until about the end of the 1970s, is a statement about use rather than about buildings and is sourced to a newspaper article. What proportion of this hall's standing timber is original and what is 1960s replication is nowhere quantified.

The road. That a Dambadeniya-period footpath ran past this hall rests on a monastic history and on older villagers' testimony, with an archaeological report for the separate route towards Anuradhapura. Whether the lane and field bund in front of the building today is a surviving stretch of it is not established. Whether Vijayabāhu I's sālā, and the catussālā of the inscriptions, are the same institution as the later ambalama is an interpretation and is presented as such by the scholars who make it.

And the obligation. No source consulted says this hall, or any particular hall, was raised under rājākariya. The documented link runs the other way: the halls are described as built for travellers going far on rājakāriya. Whether the building of them was itself a customary duty, a chieftain's endowment or a village's own initiative is described differently by different accounts and is not settled for this one.

what_to_film: Built from the ground, not the air. The hall is roughly twelve feet by nine with a ridge under twelve feet, it stands among coconut and shade trees, and the tiled hip roof hides everything structural from above. Assume no drone and find the film on foot; if a high frame is wanted at all, it is a modest elevated frame that reads the roof as one small red rectangle in a green compound, not an aerial reveal.

The roof from inside, looking up: thirty-two rafters converging on a single carved pin, held long enough that the convergence stops being clever and becomes structural. This is the shot the concept needs and it exists only from below.

The four corner boulders, the enormous squared sills laid across them, and the feet of the posts: the parts that carry weight and are not decorated, and the gap of daylight between the timber and the ground.

The carving, close and in raking morning light, one panel at a time rather than as a catalogue: the thirty-six reserved panels on the nine inner posts, the round north post with its coiled serpents and cobra hoods, the pair of wrestlers, the beam panel of a lion behind a caparisoned elephant, the sixteen-petalled lotuses on the corbels, and the rope-knots and mat-weave that repeat.

The difference in the timber itself, which the film should see rather than argue: grey weathered posts against paler replacement members carved in copy in the 1960s, and the plainer corbels among the elaborate ones.
The restoration signboard, and the compound as it actually is: the swept sand apron, the mown grass, the low boundary fence, the footpath worn to the building.
A shower arriving and the twenty minutes of noise it makes on the tiles, filmed from inside with the fields visible through the open sides.
Whoever actually stops, filmed wide and unhurried as weather rather than as portraiture, and the emptiness before and after.
The lane and the paddy tract running away from it, and any well or water source near it.
A full day compressed from first light to dark on one fixed frame, so the building's real occupancy, which is almost none, is visible.
suggested_location.access: By road from the Negombo–Kurunegala route, turning off before the town on the road toward the Matiyagane school and continuing about four kilometres; the Girīulla–Kurunegala road at Matiyagane junction and the Narammala–Kuliyapitiya road at Dangolla junction are the two approaches the archaeological literature gives. The building is a conserved monument in the care of the national archaeology department and is maintained under its Dambadeniya office, which is the office to approach; filming inside it, lighting it, and flying anything above it depend on their permission and their rules. It now sits in a kept compound with a low boundary fence and a swept sand apron, and the village lane around it is ordinary residential road that people live on. Site accounts say the villagers themselves look after it.
suggested_location.best_time: The first weeks of a monsoon, for showers in the afternoon and for standing water in the fields, and because the roof is tiled the rain has a sound worth recording from underneath. Within a day, the first hour after sunrise for raking light across the carved panels, the middle of the day for the interior looking up at the rafters, and last light for the hall as a frame with fields showing through it.

suggested_location.research_note:
Desk research only, 2026-09-26, and the additions are substantial. The fullest account consulted is a Sinhala archaeological article on archaeology.lk by Dilini Lakmali Meslinka, which quotes the Archaeological Commissioner's administration reports for 1960–63 directly, carries Dasanayake's tabulated catalogue of the carvings and Godakumbura's description of the roof, and traces the footpath from a monastic history. It is corroborated and contradicted in places by the encyclopaedia entry (drawing on Godakumbura's ICOMOS chapter), a heritage gazetteer, and a second gazetteer citing Anuradha and Kumari's departmental inventory of Kurunegala District. Everything structural, every carving count, the restoration history and the route now sit in historical_thread with certainty and dispute kept apart; datings, post counts and carving counts differ between sources and the variants are kept rather than averaged.

Three findings change what the file previously held. First, the roof: it is tiled, hipped and deeply eaved, so the thirty-two-rafter convergence is an interior feature and cannot be filmed from above. The earlier text describing a drone sitting over a wheel of rafters was wrong and has been corrected in place and what_to_film; the sequence's two overhead beats were left alone as instructed and need Chathura's decision. Second, the building is largely a 1960s repair: decayed members were dismantled and their carvings replicated on new timber, the originals were chemically treated and sent to the Anuradhapura museum, and some corbels were finished more plainly than the originals because of cost; it was retiled again in 2016. Third, the carvings are far richer than the file knew — thirty-six reserved panels on nine posts, upward of forty cobra carvings, eight lions, four elephants, a pair of wrestlers cut to read the same way inverted, and a circular north post with cobra hoods in place of lotus petals — and they are the film's strongest material.

The premise was tested and holds, with one sharpening. No builder, donor, patron or construction date is recorded for this hall in any source consulted; there is no inscription on it; the two folk attributions contradict each other. What can be named is the village and its korale, the Archaeological Commissioner who dismantled and rebuilt it, the scholars who catalogued its carvings, and a sister hall on the same footpath that was built in 1782 and has vanished. So the honest form of the claim is not that nobody can be named, but that everyone who can be named came afterwards.

On the obligation: no source consulted says this hall, or any hall, was raised under rājākariya. The documented link runs the other way — the halls were built for travellers going far on rājakāriya, on kin visits or on pilgrimage — and the accounts of who built them divide between a family or chieftain's endowment and the village's own hands. That division is left standing rather than resolved, because C011's prompted/unprompted axis makes it a secondary matter either way.

Coordinates are the point the encyclopaedia entry gives and should be treated as a direction, not a survey. Nobody has been approached, no permission has been sought, and nothing about filming access, lighting inside a protected monument or drone rules over it has been checked. All eight images were confirmed to exist through the Commons API and are of the site itself; the carving identifications in the captions are the encyclopaedia entry's gallery captions, not the file pages', and are attributed as such.

unknowns: No approach has been made to the archaeology department, and a conserved monument may simply be closed to a crew or to a drone. The site is maintained under the department's Dambadeniya office, which is the office to ask.

How much the hall is actually used today is unverified, and the film's fourth beat depends on it being used at least occasionally by people who are not tourists. The site photographs show a fenced compound with mown grass and a swept sand apron, which is the look of a kept monument rather than of a hall on a path.

The drone is probably the wrong tool here and the two overhead beats in the sequence need rethinking. The structure is about twelve feet by nine with a ridge under twelve feet, it stands under coconut and shade trees, and its tiled hip roof conceals the thirty-two rafters entirely from above. The wheel of rafters exists only from inside, looking up. Nothing has been checked about whether a useful high frame exists at all.

No builder, donor, date or inscription is recorded for this hall anywhere in the sources consulted, and the two folk attributions contradict each other. The film must be able to live with that rather than fill it in.
What proportion of the standing timber is original and what is 1960s replication is nowhere quantified, and it matters for how the carving is filmed and described.
Whether the lane and field bund in front of the hall is a surviving stretch of the old footpath, or an unrelated modern road, is not established in any source consulted.
